name: The four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa)
method_summary: Contentment with whatever robes, alms-food and lodging are obtained, and delight in abandoning (defilements) and in cultivation — practised after establishing morality and before meditation, as antidote to discontent and great desires.

name: Contemplation of the unlovely (aśubhā-bhāvanā)
method_summary: For one in whom passion predominates: the skeleton contemplation — visualizing one's body as a skeleton, extending the vision of skeletons to the ocean's edge and contracting it again; the beginner, the one who has mastered it, and the one whose attention has passed beyond, who holds the mind between the eyebrows.
signs_of_progress: mastery: removing the bones from the feet up to half the skull (AK 6.10)

warnings.text: The Vinaya origin story of the third pārājika tells that monks who practised the contemplation of the unlovely became disgusted with their bodies and took their lives; the Buddha then taught the peaceful mindfulness of breathing (low confidence on the parallels in each school's Vinaya).
The Kośa prescribes it specifically for those dominated by passion, and mindfulness of breathing for those dominated by discursive thought.

equivalents.note: Both are object-based meditations but distinct in the Kośa; listed only to prevent conflation.

name: Mindfulness of breathing in six phases (Abhidharmakośa)
method_summary: For one in whom discursive thought predominates: attention to the in- and out-breath in six phases — counting (gaṇanā), following (anugama), fixing (sthāna), observing (upalakṣaṇā), turning (vivarta) and purifying (pariśuddhi); it is wisdom, has wind as object, and is not found among outsiders. Natural breathing only; no retention.

equivalents.note: The Pali sixteen-step practice (MN 118) and the Kośa's six phases are different articulations of mindfulness of breathing.

name: The four applications of mindfulness (Kośa method)
method_summary: After calm is achieved: examining body, feeling, mind and dharmas first by their particular characteristics, then — in the application to dharmas with all as object — seeing them all as impermanent, suffering, empty and non-self; this leads into 'heat'.

equivalents.note: Same fourfold object; the Kośa adds the two-characteristic method and places it before the roots of penetration.

name: The four dhyānas
method_summary: Good one-pointedness of mind in four levels, with five, four, five and four factors (reasoning, investigation, joy, pleasure, concentration → … → equanimity, mindfulness, concentration, neither pain nor pleasure); each may be 'tasting' (with craving), pure, or without outflows.

warnings.text: Tasting (āsvādana) dhyāna is associated with craving and defiled; the pure and outflow-free kinds are to be cultivated.
The attainment of non-perception in the fourth dhyāna is entered by ordinary beings who mistake it for liberation.

name: The four formless attainments
method_summary: Infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, neither perception nor non-perception, reached by detachment from the lower level; the fourth is named for the weakness of perception.

name: The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)
method_summary: A stopping of mind and mental factors entered from the peak of existence by noble ones (non-returners and arhats) for the sake of peaceful dwelling; emerged from with a pure mind.
signs_of_progress: a non-returner who obtains it is a 'body-witness' (AK 6.43)

name: The four immeasurables (apramāṇa)
method_summary: Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity as antidotes to malice, harm, discontent and passion, with the aspects 'may beings be happy / free of suffering / rejoice', directed to beings of the desire realm.

warnings.text: The immeasurables do not themselves abandon the defilements (AK 8.31: 'na taiḥ prahāṇam').

name: The eight deliverances (vimokṣa)
method_summary: Two deliverances with the unlovely as object (in the first two dhyānas), the deliverance of the beautiful (fourth dhyāna), the four formless, and cessation.

name: The eight spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana)
method_summary: Mastering visual objects, small and great, beautiful and ugly, and the four colours, as extensions of the first, second and third deliverances.

name: The ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana)
method_summary: Earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, space and consciousness contemplated as all-pervading; the first eight in the fourth dhyāna with desire-realm objects, the last two formless.

equivalents.note: Pali kasiṇa, same ten in the Nikāyas; the Visuddhimagga's list replaces consciousness with light.

name: The three concentrations (doors of liberation)
method_summary: Concentration on emptiness (aspects empty, non-self), on the wishless (the remaining aspects of suffering, origin and path) and on the signless (the four aspects of cessation).

name: The eight-limbed fast-day vow (upavāsa)
method_summary: A lay person takes eight precepts from another in the morning, in a humble posture, repeating the formula, without ornaments, for one day and night: four limbs of morality (not killing, stealing, unchastity, lying), one of heedfulness (no intoxicants), three of the vow (no high beds, no ornaments/entertainment, no food after noon).

name: Going for refuge (Sarvāstivāda definition)
method_summary: Going for refuge to the Buddha, Dharma and Saṅgha, understood as the non-learner's dharmas that make a Buddha, the learner's and non-learner's dharmas that make the Saṅgha, and nirvāṇa; the entry to the lay discipline.

name: Giving and the field of merit
method_summary: Giving whose merit depends on the giver (faith etc.), the thing and the field (destiny, suffering, benefit, qualities); the highest gift is from one liberated to one liberated, or the bodhisattva's gift. The schools differ on whether gifts to the Buddha or to the Saṅgha yield more fruit.

name: Worship at stūpas (caitya)
method_summary: Offerings and honour at shrines holding relics; merit arises from the renunciation itself even though no one receives it (Kośa); the Dharmaguptakas held such offerings to bring great fruit.

warnings.text: Destroying a stūpa is one of the acts resembling the deadly acts.

name: The fortnightly observance (poṣadha)
method_summary: On the new- and full-moon days the monastics within one boundary assemble, confess offences, and one recites the prātimokṣa; laity observe the fast-day vows.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

name: The invitation at the end of the rains (pravāraṇā)
method_summary: At the close of the rains each monastic invites the community to point out faults seen, heard or suspected.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

name: The rains retreat (varṣā)
method_summary: Three months of residence in one place during the monsoon, a time of intensified practice and study.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

name: Full ordination (upasaṃpadā)
method_summary: Ordination as bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī by a formal act (motion and three proclamations) before a quorum, after going forth; for bhikṣuṇīs, dual ordination by both orders after two years as probationer.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

name: Going forth (pravrajyā)
method_summary: Leaving home: shaving the head, taking robes, the refuges and the ten novice precepts.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

name: Confession of offences (āpatti-deśanā)
method_summary: A monastic who has committed a confessable offence acknowledges it before another; required before the poṣadha.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

name: Probation and penance (parivāsa, mānatva)
method_summary: For a saṃghāvaśeṣa offence: a period of probation for concealment and six nights of penance, then rehabilitation by a quorum of twenty.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

name: The kaṭhina robe ceremony
method_summary: After the rains, cloth offered by laity is made into a robe for one monastic on behalf of the community, granting certain privileges.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

name: The ascetic practices (dhutaguṇa)
method_summary: Optional austerities: rag-robes, only three robes, alms-round without skipping houses, one meal, living in the forest, at a tree's root, in the open, in a charnel ground, the sitter's practice (not lying down), and others; twelve in the Sanskrit lists, thirteen in the Pali.
notes: Common to all the Vinayas; details and counts differ by school.

warnings.text: They are optional; the Vinaya accounts show the Buddha refusing to make forest-dwelling and similar austerities compulsory (Devadatta's demands).
